summary: Children find the area of a rectangle by tiling it with unit squares arranged in complete rows and columns, then discover that the count equals the product of the side lengths: number of rows × squares in each row (for example, 4 rows of 6 is 4 × 6 = 24 square units). The key is that multiplication GROWS from seeing the array — one side tells how many squares are in a row, the other tells how many rows — rather than being applied as a rote length-times-width rule. Work should distinguish this from going around the edge (perimeter), and show that rotation preserves area so 4×6 = 6×4.
misconceptions: Adds the side lengths (4 + 6 = 10) instead of multiplying — confusing area with perimeter.
Cannot structure the array — counts squares one by one with no sense of rows × columns, so never reaches the multiplication.
Multiplies the sides as a rote rule but cannot explain why it equals the tile count.
Miscounts rows or columns, especially when the grid is only partly drawn.

activities.title: Build the array and watch the multiplication grow
steps: Set up a rectangle 4 rows tall and 6 squares wide, adding one complete row of six unit squares at a time.
As each row is added, count on by six: 6, 12, 18, 24, and notice the running total jump by six each time.
Alongside the growing grid, build the matching statement '4 × 6' and connect it to 'four rows of six'.
Rotate the rectangle so it becomes 6 rows of 4; check that the total is still 24, showing 4 × 6 = 6 × 4.
Say in your own words why you do NOT have to count all 24 squares — each new row simply adds another six.
activities.insight: The multiplication IS the array: one factor is how many squares are in a row and the other is how many rows, so rows × squares-in-a-row gives the same total as counting every tile. Rotation preserves area, which is why 4×6 = 6×4.

activities.title: Tile and label on squared paper
steps: On squared paper, draw a rectangle (for example 4 by 6) and tile it by marking off every complete row and column so no squares are missing.
Count the squares — first by ones to confirm, then by skip-counting whole rows.
Write the matching multiplication (4 × 6 = 24 square units) beside the rectangle.
Point to which side tells 'how many squares in a row' and which tells 'how many rows'.
activities.insight: Drawing and tiling your own rectangle, then writing the multiplication, cements that the two side lengths are the per-row count and the number of rows, and that their product is the area in square units.

activities.title: Area is not the distance around (spot the error)
steps: Look at a worked attempt where a child wrote 4 + 6 = 10 as the 'area' of a 4-by-6 rectangle.
Decide what 4 + 6 actually measures, and correct the method to find the true area.
Trace the border of the rectangle to see that adding sides follows the edge, while tiling covers the surface.
Rebuild the array and state the correct area, 24 square units, with its multiplication.
activities.insight: Adding two side lengths (4 + 6 = 10) measures along the edge, not the covered surface; even the full border (4 + 6 + 4 + 6 = 20) is still a length around, not area. Area is the count of unit squares that fill the rectangle, found by multiplying squares-in-a-row by number-of-rows.

activities.title: Row-strips that fill the rectangle
steps: Take strips of six joined unit squares (row-strips) and lay them to fill a 4-by-6 rectangle with no gaps or overlaps.
Count how many strips are needed (4), and how many squares each strip holds (6).
Skip-count the strips — 6, 12, 18, 24 — to find the total.
Write and say the multiplication: four rows of six is 4 × 6 = 24 square units.
activities.insight: Repeated equal row-strips make the 'rows × number-in-each-row' structure physical, so the multiplication is felt as grouping equal rows rather than a memorised rule.

activities.title: Check and justify the link
steps: Answer why 4 × 6 gives the same number as counting all the tiles one by one, pointing to 'squares in a row' and 'number of rows'.
Complete a statement such as '4 × 6 = __ square units' and explain the unit.
Compare a 4×6 and a rotated 6×4 rectangle and state whether the area changes, with a reason.
Explain what a classmate measured if they wrote 4 + 6 = 10 for the area.
activities.insight: Being able to justify the multiplication — not just compute it — is the sign the array structure has become the reason for the formula.

checkQuestion: Give the child a rectangle (e.g. 4 by 6) on squared paper or with unit-square tiles and say: 'Tile this, find its area, and show me why the area equals the side lengths multiplied together.' Watch whether they build rows and columns or count one by one, whether they multiply or add the sides, and whether they can explain the link.
checkAnswer: The child tiles the rectangle in complete rows and columns with no gaps, finds the area (24) by counting or skip-counting rows, writes 4 × 6 = 24, and explains that one side gives the number of squares in a row and the other gives the number of rows — so multiplying them gives the same total as counting all the tiles.
